The post Review: Wines of Iterum, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Joe Dobbes is an icon in Oregon’s Willamette Valley, whose wineries Dobbes Family Estate and Wine by Joe have been staples of the region for decades. Iterum is Dobbes’s self-proclaimed “retirement project,” a prestige brand founded in 2019 that draws on Dobbes’s deep knowledge of Oregon terroir and features numerous single vineyard expressions in its arsenal.

The bottles are quirky — they don’t even note the varietal on the front label — but that only adds to their significant charm.

Thoughts on four new releases follow. 2022 is the current vintage for most of these wines.

2024 Iterum Estate Sauvignon Blanc Orchard House Vineyard – Remarkably expressive for sauvignon blanc (though not an iconic offering from Willamette), this is a fruit-forward expression of a classic style, with upfront notes of apricot and peach layered with saline and, later, coconut cream, chased by lemon curd. The lattermost of these offers a decidedly tart character to the finish, though the lemon meringue pie quality finds a tempering note in late-arriving notes of crushed graham crackers and some toasted coconut. Dessert is served. A- / $50

2022 Iterum Estate Chardonnay Orchard House Vineyard – The pale straw color of this wine is misleading, as it’s a fairly classically structured chardonnay, though the oak and vanilla are kept in check by terraced layers of lemon peel, grapefruit, and mild notes of guava. The body is rich and exotic, and it would evoke the best wedding cake you’d ever had if there was more sugar in the mix, but fortunately there’s not. Instead, a bright acidity brings the finish to a slightly salty crescendo, with echoes of lemon, almond, and orchids draped around the neck. A- / $75

2022 Iterum Estate Pinot Noir “Old Friend” Quailhurst – This Chehalem Mountains AVA bottling surprised right away with its boldly earthy attack, gravelly and almost muddy, any sense of fruit requiring a lengthy spell in glass before it reveals itself. When it does, dried cherries and prunes force their way forward to eventually dominate, layered with dark chocolate, graphite, and ashy creosote. The experience remains heady, almost overwhelming, the weight of its massive body a leaden twist on the pinot formula. Time in glass helps loosen the threads a bit, but this takes a significant amount of patience. B / $90

2022 Iterum Estate Pinot Noir “Old Friend” Symonette Vineyard – A vibrant and far different pinot than the Quailhurst bottling, this Eola-Amity Hills expression is a lithe expression of Oregon pinot noir at its very best: Bright cherry fruit, layered with both raspberry and strawberry, is chased by soothing notes of black tea, followed by the lightest dusting of crushed slate and powdered anise. The earthier notes complement a lively fruit attack, the finish finding a deft balance between the two halves, concluding with an echo of fruit tea, ever so slightly exuding a minerally dust. It goes on and on forever, back and forth, back and forth. One of my favorite pinots in recent memory, I love this stuff. A / $90

title: Review: Pegasus Vodka and Eau d’Or
summary:
We previously reviewed Pegasus Distillery’s meteorite-infused vodka, but today we circle around to try their more grounded, original vodka along with the citrus focused liqueur Eau d’Or. Both are made at the Meursault, Burgundy-located distillery, which is still fairly young, having been founded in 2021, but they are drawing attention by making exciting products with…

The post Review: Pegasus Vodka and Eau d’Or appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We previously reviewed Pegasus Distillery’s meteorite-infused vodka, but today we circle around to try their more grounded, original vodka along with the citrus focused liqueur Eau d’Or. Both are made at the Meursault, Burgundy-located distillery, which is still fairly young, having been founded in 2021, but they are drawing attention by making exciting products with technologically advanced distilling and certified organic ingredients. More details about the distillery and their practices can be found in our reviews of their unusual vodka and Orion Gin.

Pegasus Vodka Review

As with their Orion Gin, Pegasus Vodka is also made using their iStill, which mashes, ferments, and distills at once. The vodka is made from certified organic French wheat, using spring water sourced deep underground, beneath the distillery. On the nose, the vodka is quite clean, offering some gentle, pleasant cereal aromas and a light hospital note. The palate is more assertive, opening with sweet, maybe too sweet cereal grains that were not present on the nose. With time, further notes begin to appear, including lemon drop, vanilla, and minerality. The vodka has a lovely, oily mouthfeel and a very long finish as the flavors and the sweetness slowly dissipate. The sweetness will be a determining factor for this vodka; if that sweetness resonates with you, it stands as an excellent choice for cocktails or even for sipping neat. 80 proof. B / $35

Pegasus Eau d’Or Review

We have to start with the bottle, which is really quite attractive and would make a lovely gift. The liqueur inside the bottle was reportedly inspired by an original recipe of Louis XIV’s reign, and it is distilled with French organic lemons, bitter oranges, and orange blossom from Menton on the French Riviera. Pegasus distillery explains their dynamic maceration process: “Each citrus undergoes an 18-hour dynamic maceration with five successive passes to progressively extract essential oils and aromatic compounds. It is then re-distilled for 12 hours to refine fragrance and structure.”

The result is an assertive, sweet citrus liqueur.

Poured neat in the glass, Eau d’Or introduces bold, sweet aromas of candied oranges and lemons along with a bit of a floral note. The palate is more of the same. Oily sweet orange rind hits first, with lemon pith following. The flavors are quite strong but not overpowering, sweet but not too sweet, which is to say: This is a well-balanced liqueur. A slight alcohol bite comes at the end, which I enjoyed after the sweetness faded.

This liqueur is intended for cocktails, but I could imagine drinking it in lieu of dessert, perhaps with just an ice cube. On their website, they recommend drinking it with seltzer or tonic, and it goes beautifully with both for a refreshing, low-abv cocktail option. They also suggest cocktails that include both the vodka and the liqueur along with other ingredients. I tried just mixing the two and found that they go together nicely, making for a well-rounded orange vodka martini. 46 proof. A- / $35

title: Review: Whiskeys of Locke + Co.
summary:
Colorado-based Locke + Co. — with a plus, not an ampersand — appears to be following in the footsteps of other mountainous distillers by forging its own path. Focusing on bourbon and rye releases, the busy operation has a singular trick up its sleeve that it leans on for all of its releases to date:…

The post Review: Whiskeys of Locke + Co. appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Colorado-based Locke + Co. — with a plus, not an ampersand — appears to be following in the footsteps of other mountainous distillers by forging its own path. Focusing on bourbon and rye releases, the busy operation has a singular trick up its sleeve that it leans on for all of its releases to date: Finishing with aspen wood.

The details of this finishing vary from one release to the next, but largely it involves tanking fully mature whiskey (aged in new charred oak) and adding aspen discs for a while before bottling. The way those discs are treated and the length of time they spend in the finishing tank aren’t standard, but Locke’s love affair with the evergreen tree is a constant.

We received three of Locke’s most prominent, permanent releases. Thoughts follow.

Locke + Co. Big Catch Bourbon Review

Made from a blend of high rye and high wheat bourbon mashbills (making this a four grain release), this is aged two years in new Missouri oak barrels before finishing in tanks on both new charred aspen wood discs and rye-soaked charred aspen discs.

The nose comes across as significantly more mature than its mere 2 year old age would suggest, the wood aromas coming across as evergreen and refreshing, lacking the lumberyard heft one might expect at this age. An herbal note takes things into more minty territory in time — clearly that aspen finishing has had a massive impact on the final product.

The palate is softer and quieter than the nose by a wide margin, which is perhaps to be expected as the underlying whiskey doesn’t have enough maturity to back up the woodsy treatment. It’s still a lively experience and a well-crafted bourbon, though it simply comes across as short. A gentle peanut-popcorn attack sees a smear of vanilla and a touch of maple, chased by a light layer of peppery char. While gently sweet on the finish, I found myself really missing the aspen impact that’s so vibrant on the nose. 95 proof. B+ / $52

Locke + Co. Big Blaze Bourbon Review

While I wouldn’t personally choose to name two very different products “Big X,” that’s a story for another time. This one is aged for 5 years (mashbill unstated), then finished with aspen discs that were harvested from trees that naturally burned in a 2020 Colorado forest fire (hence the name).

Bolder and more immersive on the nose, this whiskey has a different aspen influence that has more of a torched nose, smoldering evergreen branches mixed with a more straightforward grassiness, later somewhat hemp-like, or evocative of coconut husk. The whiskey has a certain nuttiness in evidence, but the aroma gravitates toward smoke the longer it sits in glass.

The palate melds tradition with the impact of the unique finish — fairly heavy on the peanuts up front, mild vanilla, then more of a Butterfinger flavor as the finish builds. A little time in glass sees the evergreen element vanishing almost completely; here we see the opposite of Big Catch, where the added age on the whiskey has effectively subdued the impact of the finish. All told, it’s a lively bourbon, though it lacks the clear distinction of its little brother. 95 proof. B / $57

Locke + Co. Aspen Aged Rye Review

This rye (no mashbill supplied) is aged for “three plus” years in new half-size 30-gallon oak barrels with a variety of char levels: 2, 3, 4, and 5. After that, the whiskey is tanked and finished on charred Colorado aspen discs for 8 months.

This noses with the most classic profile of this trio of whiskeys, a very herbal, grassy aroma bursting from the glass, quite extreme at times. The whiskey smolders with crispy burnt edges in the glass, though the longer it sits, the more these aromas burn off. (So to speak.)

The palate has the bright greenness of lots of rye — fresh (not dried) hay, just-mown lawn. It doesn’t surprise much, though there’s a latent sweetness evocative of coconut nectar and a pinch of cloves on the finish, both of which serve to cut at least a bit through the lingering flavors of cut grass. 90 proof. B / $70 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Blue Note Cherry Wood Cask Bourbon
summary:
Blue Note Bourbon was initially launched in mid-July 2018 by B.R. Distilling Company in Memphis, Tennessee. As an Owensboro resident, Blue Note has held a special place in my appreciation of my city’s whiskey story. During the early days of whiskey distilling’s revival in Owensboro, O.Z. Tyler was giving consumers very young bourbon that had…

The post Review: Blue Note Cherry Wood Cask Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Blue Note Bourbon was initially launched in mid-July 2018 by B.R. Distilling Company in Memphis, Tennessee. As an Owensboro resident, Blue Note has held a special place in my appreciation of my city’s whiskey story.

During the early days of whiskey distilling’s revival in Owensboro, O.Z. Tyler was giving consumers very young bourbon that had been rapidly aged through the infamous TerrePure process. Before O.Z. Tyler transitioned to Green River Distilling, and before Green River began offering traditionally aged bourbon with a respectable period of maturation under the Green River name, Blue Note was already giving consumers traditionally aged bourbon distilled in Owensboro.

For me, that made Blue Note one of the earliest opportunities to see what Owensboro-distilled bourbon could offer without the influence of the TerrePure process. Years later, Blue Note continues to experiment with bourbon distilled in Owensboro, with its latest release taking that work in an unusual direction.

In August 2026, B.R. Distilling released Blue Note Cherry Wood Cask Bourbon. The Owensboro-distilled bourbon starts with a mashbill of 70% corn, 21% rye, and 9% malted barley. A total of 27 barrels of bourbon, aged between five and six years, were blended and transferred into 22 cherry wood barrels. Those barrels received either heavy or medium toasting before the bourbon spent just over four additional months in the cherry wood.

The cherry wood barrels were filled in early spring and dumped during the summer. They were made from sustainably harvested wild cherry wood sourced from the Jura region of eastern France.

The casks came from Prunus avium L., known as “merisier” in French. The French National Forest Office, or ONF, identifies merisier specifically as Prunus avium, the wild ancestor of cultivated sweet cherries.

Wild cherry fruit has a long history of use in spirits, including kirsch and cherry brandy. Prunus avium is also highly prized for furniture and woodworking, making its use in bourbon maturation an interesting extension of the wood’s long history.

There is also an interesting chemical connection. Sakuranin is the most abundant volatile compound identified in wild cherry extract, adding another point of reference when considering the 2026 “Sakura cask” bourbon releases from Starlight and Pursuit Spirits, which have been marketed around Japanese cherry trees.

So, what do France’s wild cherry trees do for bourbon?

Blue Note Cherry Wood Cask Bourbon Review

The nose opens with cranberry juice, bringing a combination of sweetness and tartness, followed almost immediately by toasted almonds. As the initial aromas recede, Swedish Fish candy enters the picture, with artificial raspberry and cherry joined by a touch of citrus. Graham cracker ties the aromas together, adding a baked sweetness to the fruit. The nose is decidedly sweet, with an emphasis on dark red fruit that should appeal to bourbon drinkers who favor this particular profile.

The palate follows suit, with amaretto leading the way alongside sweet apricot jam. The opening is dominated by fruit and sweetness, but ginger and white pepper bring a spicy turn through the mid-palate. Despite the change in flavor, the mouthfeel remains notably oily.

The finish is where the bourbon takes an unexpected turn. A touch of tannic plum skin appears first, soon giving way to more red fruit in the form of Cheerwine. That sweetness then gives way to grape seeds, bringing the tannins needed to offset the fruit. The trouble is that the grape seed bitterness pushes a little too far, leaving more bitterness than I would prefer at the end of a sip.

This is an intriguing bourbon built around sweet, dark red fruit, with cranberry, cherry, and raspberry setting the tone from nose to palate. The finish, however, tells a different story, ending on a pronounced bitter note that detracts from an otherwise enjoyable tasting experience.

119.4 proof.

B+ / $65

title: Review: Elysian Punkuccino
summary:
Take a seasonal pumpkin ale and mix it with a classic milk stout and what do you get? This surprisingly delightful blend of beer styles that is built around a complex mix of Stumptown cold brew coffee, cinnamon, nutmeg, lactose, various malts, German Northern Brewer hops, and three different additions of pumpkin to the…

The post Review: Elysian Punkuccino appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Take a seasonal pumpkin ale and mix it with a classic milk stout and what do you get? This surprisingly delightful blend of beer styles that is built around a complex mix of Stumptown cold brew coffee, cinnamon, nutmeg, lactose, various malts, German Northern Brewer hops, and three different additions of pumpkin to the kettle.

It’s a near-perfect mix of both coffee and pumpkin spice flavors, heavy on the nutmeg up front, giving the attack a distinct gingerbread quality. The coffee rolls in quickly from there, though it’s amply balanced by hops to keep it from taking over completely. As the malts join the party, the beer bounces among a trinity of elements — pumpkin cake, milky coffee, and the doughy essence of a lightly hopped lager. Any one of these on their own may not have impressed, but what Elysian has done in the combination is nothing short of genius. Probably my favorite autumn brew I’ve tasted to date.

6% abv.

A- / $7 per 22 oz bottle (cans typically available in mixed packs)

summary:

The premise remains rooted in Alpine traditions: Teroldego and Marzemino are harvested off hillside vineyards in the…

The post Review: 2025 Mezzacorona Dinotte Red Blend appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Mezzacorona’s Ventessa lineup already made its case for Trentino as a place worth considering when looking for a proper budget wine buy, so Dinotte was presumably christened for mood rather than any darkness in the glass or otherwise.

The premise remains rooted in Alpine traditions: Teroldego and Marzemino are harvested off hillside vineyards in the granite-heavy Dolomites, with the altitude performing labor usually attributed to the winemaker rather than the mountain. Then, for a bit of complexity, a bit of Merlot is thrown into the mix. Cool nights at that elevation produce brightness in the bottle, one of those  claims in the wine trade that sounds like a sales pitch until the glass proves it isn’t. What shows up are aromas of blackberry and red currant, tempered by French oak. There’s a savory streak running through the palate, with pencil lead and granite supporting the darker fruit. Touches of anise, clove and nutmeg cut through on the finish as the fruit recedes. It pairs quite well with a quality piece of dark chocolate or a small charcuterie board, but can also stand firmly on its own.

B / $11

Guitar makers have used whiskey barrel wood for years. With Tonewood, Whiskey Jypsi and Gibson flipped the idea: toasted maple tonewood offcuts from Gibson’s broader guitar-building process, wood already prized…

The post Review: Whiskey Jypsi Gibson Tonewood: The Collective appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Here’s a new collaboration for you: Whiskey Jypsi partnered with Gibson — the guitar makers — to “reverse the familiar relationship between guitars and whiskey. Guitar makers have used whiskey barrel wood for years. With Tonewood, Whiskey Jypsi and Gibson flipped the idea: toasted maple tonewood offcuts from Gibson’s broader guitar-building process, wood already prized for resonance and character, are reimagined for whiskey finishing.” The release coincides with the launch of a new Eric Church guitar called The Epiphone, though its details are beyond the scope of Drinkhacker’s coverage, I fear.

There are two Tonewood whiskeys coming out. The first is a very limited offering (250 bottles) called Tonewood: Vol. 1, made from 20 and 14 year old whiskey stocks finished with toasted Gibson maple offcuts. The second is a more available spirit called Tonewood: The Collective, reviewed here, which uses younger whiskey stocks — 36% 14-year-old American whiskey from a bourbon mashbill (84% corn / 8% rye / 8% malted barley) and 64% 8-year-old straight bourbon (75% corn / 21% rye / 4% malted barley) — as its base. It’s finished on those same Gibson maple offcuts.

Whiskey Jypsi Gibson Tonewood: The Collective Review

The nose here is clean and quite sweet, the maple influence obvious from the get-go. Gently infused with gingery baking spices, a syrupy aroma emerges in short order, evoking Sunday pancakes with a side of chocolate milk. Oak is toasty and soothing, well-integrated into a pleasant and rounded whole. Indeed, it smells exactly what you imagine a freshly constructed acoustic guitar might smell like.

The palate continues the theme, and is perhaps even sweeter than the nose suggests, the maple quickly ceding way to notes of milk chocolate, then some mint. Caramel and toffee build from there, though eventually they give way to a more bready, toasty quality that grips the finish. Combined with the lingering spice notes and the not insignificant sweetness, the whiskey ultimately gives the impression of cinnamon rolls, though a touch of cayenne adds just the lightest sense of heat to the fade-out.

Solid, to be sure, but it’s firmly sweet tooth material.

103 proof.

A- / $199

summary:

Both are available in standard bottles and in 187ml “splits” that can be…

The post Review: NV Nicolas Feuillatte Brut and Rose Champagne (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We’ve written about the Champagnes of Nicolas Feuillatte several times, but here’s a fresh look at two of the operation’s most available bottlings from the “Reserve Exclusive” series — a nonvintage brut and a rose, both seen here in their 2020 incarnations. Both are available in standard bottles and in 187ml “splits” that can be consumed with nothing more than a straw.

Update 2026: We’re looking at these iconic bottles through a fresh lens, six years later.

NV Nicolas Feuillatte Reserve Exclusive Brut Champagne (2020) – There’s lots of toasty brioche up top, then a lively fruit component comes into focus. Apples and pears, plus a tropical spin, give this Brut lots of crispness and life, but the orchard notes fade away in fairly short order, leaving behind a reprise of toasted bread and a hint of Christmas spice. A- / $39 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE]

NV Nicolas Feuillatte Reserve Exclusive Brut Champagne (2026) – The Champagne’s house style is very much intact. The nose shows apple, pear, lemon drop, and lightly buttered brioche. The palate follows the nose with well-integrated notes of apple, pear, and toast. It is slightly sweet but that comes from the fruit, and it is certainly not cloying. As Chris noted tasting an earlier bottle, the finish is a bit short. But the bubbles are small and plentiful, providing a lovely, silky mouthfeel and there is medium to high acidity, promising this will pair with food nicely. -RL A- / $39 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE]

NV Nicolas Feuillatte Reserve Exclusive Rose Champagne (2020) – Less overwhelmingly fruity than you might expect, with notes of carnations, roses, and marshmallow fluff dominating. At the same time, it’s not particularly sweet, though a cherry and strawberry character on the back end work well with the creamy character up top. Less “serious” than the Brut, but certainly summery and festive. A- / $56 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE]

NV Nicolas Feuillatte Reserve Exclusive Brut Rosé Champagne (2026) – A nose showing enjoyable aromas of lemon icing on buttery shortbread. The mousse is aggressive, offering a torrent of small bubbles, maybe too much. With a little time in the glass, they start to settle down, but fans may find the effusive effervescence a plus. The palate follows the nose, with bright lemon citrus coming first and yeasty brioche following. The wine shows medium acidity, and it will both pair nicely with food and be enjoyable on its own. -RL A- / $70 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE]

title: Review: Non-Alcoholic Wines from French Bloom
summary:
Non-alcoholic wine can still feel like an immense leap of faith. It’s a perpetual trust-fall exercise, hoping whoever is on the other side bottling the stuff actually cares that it tastes like something in the same postal code as the alcohol-filled alternative. Enter French Bloom, a venture co-founded by ex-Michelin guide director Maggie Frerejean-Taittinger and…

The post Review: Non-Alcoholic Wines from French Bloom appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Non-alcoholic wine can still feel like an immense leap of faith. It’s a perpetual trust-fall exercise, hoping whoever is on the other side bottling the stuff actually cares that it tastes like something in the same postal code as the alcohol-filled alternative. Enter French Bloom, a venture co-founded by ex-Michelin guide director Maggie Frerejean-Taittinger and model Constance Jablonski, arriving with a pair of options timed almost with precision to the entire grueling holiday gauntlet, and the inevitable cleansing of Dry January. They are also the official non-alcoholic sparkling wine of Formula 1, a sport whose relationship to sobriety seems complicated by the customary champagne showers in the winner’s circle.

NV French Bloom Le Rosé – Filled with rose petal and red berry character, followed by notes of guava and white peach on the palate. There’s a curious blend of white tea and rhubarb lingering on the finish, providing a tart pinch as it fades. The mouthfeel is about as close to bubbly as it can get, though. A nice Sunday brunch accompaniment, especially when served with a sliced strawberry as garnish. B+ / $44

NV French Bloom Le Blanc – There’s some complexity working here: nuts, Granny Smith apple, a little honey, and an oxidative thing happening, reading as intentional rather than a bottle gone rogue. The palate leans into apple crumble territory, but the middle sags the way anything missing non-alcoholic tends to sag, as a tent with one pole pulled. It finishes quite tart with a touch of lemon zest, propped up entirely by acid doing the heavy lifting alcohol usually handles. B+ / $39

title: Review: Angel’s Envy Cellar Collection Rye Finished in Peach Brandy and Toasted Oak Barrels
summary:
Angel’s Envy has built its reputation on the idea that a whiskey’s journey need not end with its initial maturation. Since the introduction of its port finished bourbon, the Louisville-based whiskey maker has explored the effects of secondary maturation, from the Caribbean rum casks used for its rye whiskey, first released in 2013, to the…

The post Review: Angel’s Envy Cellar Collection Rye Finished in Peach Brandy and Toasted Oak Barrels appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Angel’s Envy has built its reputation on the idea that a whiskey’s journey need not end with its initial maturation. Since the introduction of its port finished bourbon, the Louisville-based whiskey maker has explored the effects of secondary maturation, from the Caribbean rum casks used for its rye whiskey, first released in 2013, to the more unusual cask combinations featured in its limited releases.

For Volume 6 of the Angel’s Envy Cellar Collection, Master Distiller Owen Martin pulls out all the stops, bringing together peach brandy casks, toasted American oak, and toasted French oak. The foundation is rye whiskey made from a mashbill of 95% rye and 5% malted barley. Unlike Angel’s Envy’s standard rye, which was distilled in Indiana, this release draws on whiskey from two undisclosed Kentucky distilleries. The result is a meeting of grain, fruit, and wood, with three different finishing regimens shaping the final blend.

The whiskey was initially barreled between June 2014 and March 2018. Before secondary maturation, the youngest component spent 6 years, 6 months, and 6 days in oak, while the oldest aged for 11 years, 5 months, and 24 days. Following their respective finishes, the whiskeys were blended, bringing the total time spent in oak to between 8 and 11 years.

The younger component was finished primarily in toasted oak casks. The older component spent most of its finishing period in peach brandy casks, though some of it also went into toasted oak. In the final blend, 54.5% consists of whiskey aged for at least eight years, while the remaining 45.5% comprises whiskey aged between 10 and 11 years.

Peach brandy-finished whiskey accounts for 37.7% of the blend. Another 35.4% was finished in first- and second-fill toasted French oak casks, while the remaining 26.9% spent its finishing period in toasted American oak.

The peach brandy casks are 53 gallon ex-bourbon barrels that previously held peach brandy for at least three years. The brandy was distilled from a variety of clingstone peaches, primarily Dixon and Halford, along with freestone varieties, mainly Elberta and Big Red. The rye whiskey spent 15 to 23 months in these casks, entering at 114.5 proof.

Meanwhile, the toasted French and American oak finishes lasted between six and 12 months in custom heavy-toast barrels supplied by Kelvin Cooperage and Independent Stave Company. The whiskey entered these casks at 112.4 proof. After blending, the whiskey reached a natural harvest proof of 110.

With nearly a decade or more in oak for much of the blend, three finishing regimens, and peach brandy made from several varieties of peaches, Angel’s Envy has assembled an unusual take on Kentucky rye whiskey. How does this union of rye, peach brandy, and toasted oak turn out? Is it a little slice of Heaven in a glass? Let’s find out!

Angel’s Envy Cellar Collection Rye Finished in Peach Brandy and Toasted Oak Barrels Review

The nose opens with mildly sweet tea and honey. The sweetness is present, though likely not enough to satisfy many Southerners. Peach brandy makes its presence known without pushing the whiskey into overly sweet territory. Nutmeg joins the bouquet, accompanied by a floral note of orange blossom. As the whiskey sits in the glass, dusty oak arrives late, adding another dimension to the nose. I appreciate how clearly the peach brandy casks make their mark without dominating the whiskey.

On the palate, the peach brandy influence is immediate, though the fruit is less juicy, skewing a bit earthy, bringing to mind dehydrated peaches. A mild cinnamon note follows, with a natural spice quality rather than the artificial flavor of cinnamon gum. The mid-palate introduces cantaloupe, joined by ginger spice, with a pleasantly dry mouthfeel.

The finish brings more oak to the forefront, along with a brief sensation of chewing on a No. 2 pencil. That quickly gives way to cantaloupe rind and white pepper before circling back to the earthy, dried peach note found earlier in the tasting.

I consider this release a major success. Finishing whiskey in multiple cask types can easily result in one influence overpowering the others, but Owen Martin has brought together peach brandy, toasted French oak, and toasted American oak to excellent effect. Each finishing regimen makes its presence known without overwhelming the others. The result is an unusual, high-quality rye whiskey that, in my estimation, justifies its price.
